Summary
Data source overview: This paper (Measuring and Avoiding Side Effects Using Relative Reachability, 2019) analyses why existing generic techniques for preventing harmful side-effects in reinforcement-learning (RL) agents fail, articulates four formal desiderata for any side-effect measure, proposes the “relative reachability” penalty that compares the reachability of all states from the current state to an inaction-baseline, introduces several computable variants of the penalty, and validates the approach on three grid-world environments, showing better safety performance than prior penalties.

EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[87]  
The paper presents clear causal reasoning from the identified risk through design to empirical validation. Instructions were followed closely; all core reasoning steps were decomposed, framework internals made explicit, node granularity kept merge-friendly, and every node is connected. Potential improvements: provide explicit examples of acceptable edge confidences and a canonical list of baseline section-title formats to reference in node/edge rationales.  

Inference strategy justification: Moderate inference was only used to phrase interventions that are straightforward applications of the validated penalty. All such edges are marked confidence 2.  

Extraction completeness explanation: 15 carefully chosen nodes capture every distinct claim on the causal path from the top-level risk through limitations of prior work → formal desiderata → new measure → concrete formulations → empirical findings → practicable interventions.  

Key limitations: 1) Empirical evidence is limited to toy domains—edge confidences reflect this. 2) Implementation details for large-scale systems are theoretical; intervention maturity is therefore low. 3) Baseline-choice research gaps noted by authors are not converted into interventions because no concrete method was offered.
